newsitem.title: USA: Court upholds IBM pact to end consent decree.
newsitem.headline: Court upholds IBM pact to end consent decree.

text.p: A federal judge approved an agreement between International Business Machines Corp. and the Justice Department that will dissolve the rest of a 1956 consent decree that had hampered IBM in the computer services business, the company said Thursday.

"We reached a settlement last July with the Justice Department that would sunset the remainder of the decree," an IBM spokeswoman said. "Yesterday, U.S. District Judge Thomas Griesa approved the settlement."
In a court filing, the New York-based judge wrote the agreement between IBM and the department will "benefit both IBM and consumers."

The consent decree, which resulted from antitrust action brought against the computer giant in 1952, has forced IBM to segregate its computer services operations into a separate unit which must pay full retail price for equipment and software it buys from IBM to resell to customers.

The decree was greatly modified in Jaunary 1996 after an agreement between Armonk, N.Y.-based IBM and the government, but there were several remaining provisions that hurt IBM. One requires IBM to offer computers for sale at terms comparable to those applicable to customers who are leasing the systems.

Another provision placed limitations on the ability of IBM to reacquire and resell computer equipment originally sold by it. IBM was also forbidden from discriminating in providing maintenance services in favor of its lessees and against purchasers and third-party repair companies.

Provisions regarding restrictions on spare parts and maintenance of IBM's AS/400 minicomputer line will terminate July 2, 2000, and the remaining restrictions on its System/390 mainframe line will terminate July 2, 2001. These provisions forbid IBM from requiring that a computer purchaser obtain spare parts or maintenance services from IBM.
In upholding the agreement, Judge Griesa wrote that the government and IBM had amassed a great deal of information about the current competitive position of IBM in the marketplace.
"The situation has changed drastically in the 40 years since the time the consent decree was entered," Griesa wrote.

"It has been established beyond any real question that, whereas IBM formerly had a great degree of market power in an antitrust sense, that market power has been substantially diminished, and is continuing to diminish, to the point of disappearance in the sense of a threat of antitrust violation," he wrote.
The IBM spokeswoman said the company believes it will save millions of dollars as a result of the end of the consent decree, which placed "huge administrative burdens" on IBM.
